title: AI software on a Fire and Rescue NSW drone detects two lost hikers off the Dead Horse Gap track, and they are located within five hours
summary: On a Fire and Rescue NSW drone, AI software from a vendor that no source names flagged two lost hikers in Kosciuszko National Park, and they were located within five hours.
account: On Tuesday 23 June 2026 two men in their early 20s failed to reach a rendezvous on the Dead Horse Gap walking track. The track is in Kosciuszko National Park, about 35 km south-west of Jindabyne. They were reported overdue at about 7 pm. NSW Police formed an alpine search team with the State Emergency Service and asked Fire and Rescue NSW for drone support. Fire and Rescue NSW launched a remotely piloted aircraft with thermal imaging and AI detection software. The software flagged the pair in bushland about 500 m off the track, and the thermal camera confirmed the find. The drone's spotlight directed ground crews to them. They were located less than five hours after the report, had mild effects of exposure and declined treatment. Inspector Phillip Eberle of Fire and Rescue NSW later told About Regional that rescuers took about four hours to reach the pair after the find and guided them to safety around midnight. Fire and Rescue NSW described the rescue in a media release on 25 June 2026. On 27 June 2026 ABC News reported that Inspector Eberle said that the technology turned a potential long-term incident into a short-term one. ABC also reported that Inspector Eberle said that the technology probably reduced the search by several days. Fire and Rescue NSW chief remote pilot Inspector Russell Turner told ABC News that the drones were part of a statewide technology upgrade introduced over the previous 18 months. ABC reports that this was the first time that Fire and Rescue NSW had used the drone's AI detection to find a missing hiker.
purpose: Built to detect people, vehicles and vessels in drone imagery for search and rescue; this benefit is that purpose.
system: Fire and Rescue NSW remotely piloted aircraft system with thermal imaging and AI person-detection software (software vendor not named in the sources)
location: Dead Horse Gap track, Kosciuszko National Park, New South Wales, Australia (about 35 km south-west of Jindabyne)

ratings.reason: Two young men lost on a winter night in alpine bushland were found with mild exposure within five hours. The inspector overseeing the search said that it could otherwise have become a long-term incident.
Fire and Rescue NSW, the police and the State Emergency Service avoided an overnight search by several agencies and the risk to rescuers that Inspector Eberle described.

ai_role.statement: The AI flagged the hikers in the drone feed, and the thermal camera confirmed the find. The inspector overseeing the search credits it with cutting the search short. The hikers also signaled with a phone light, and the software vendor is not named. FRNSW’s June 25, 2026 release confirms that AI flagged the pair, thermal imaging verified the detection, and the spotlight guided rescuers. The release also records their phone-light signal.

fields.title: AI software on a Fire and Rescue NSW drone detects two lost hikers off the Dead Horse Gap track, and they are located within five hours
fields.headline: Drone software detects two lost hikers, who are found within five hours

value.role: SHA-256 of the complete public record and its assessments

fields.account: On Tuesday 23 June 2026 two men in their early 20s failed to reach a rendezvous on the Dead Horse Gap walking track. The track is in Kosciuszko National Park, about 35 km south-west of Jindabyne. They were reported overdue at about 7 pm. NSW Police formed an alpine search team with the State Emergency Service and asked Fire and Rescue NSW for drone support. Fire and Rescue NSW launched a remotely piloted aircraft with thermal imaging and AI detection software. The software flagged the pair in bushland about 500 m off the track, and the thermal camera confirmed the find. The drone's spotlight directed ground crews to them. They were located less than five hours after the report, had mild effects of exposure and declined treatment. Inspector Phillip Eberle of Fire and Rescue NSW later told About Regional that rescuers took about four hours to reach the pair after the find and guided them to safety around midnight. Fire and Rescue NSW described the rescue in a media release on 25 June 2026. On 27 June 2026 ABC News reported that Inspector Eberle said that the technology turned a potential long-term incident into a short-term one. ABC also reported that Inspector Eberle said that the technology probably reduced the search by several days. Fire and Rescue NSW chief remote pilot Inspector Russell Turner told ABC News that the drones were part of a statewide technology upgrade introduced over the previous 18 months. ABC reports that this was the first time that Fire and Rescue NSW had used the drone's AI detection to find a missing hiker.
